source: According to usage they were pumping the ship next morning; and lo! no inconsiderable oil came up with the water; the casks below must have sprung a bad leak. Much concern was shown; and Starbuck went down into the cabin to report this unfavourable affair.*

*In Sperm-whalemen with any considerable quantity of oil on board, it is a regular semi-weekly duty to conduct a hose into the hold, and drench the casks with sea-water; which afterwards, at varying intervals, is removed by the ship’s pumps. Hereby the casks are sought to be kept damply tight; while by the changed character of the withdrawn water, the mariners readily detect any serious leakage in the precious cargo.

Now, from the South and West the Pequod was drawing nigh to Formosa and the Bashee Isles, between which lies one of the tropical outlets from the China waters into the Pacific. And so Starbuck found Ahab with a general chart of the oriental archipelagoes spread before him; and another separate one representing the long eastern coasts of the Japanese islands—Niphon, Matsmai, and Sikoke. With his snow-white new ivory leg braced against the screwed leg of his table, and with a long pruning-hook of a jack-knife in his hand, the wondrous old man, with his back to the gangway door, was wrinkling his brow, and tracing his old courses again.
“Who’s there?” hearing the footstep at the door, but not turning round to it. “On deck! Begone!”
“Captain Ahab mistakes; it is I. The oil in the hold is leaking, sir. We must up Burtons and break out.”
“Up Burtons and break out? Now that we are nearing Japan; heave-to here for a week to tinker a parcel of old hoops?”
“Either do that, sir, or waste in one day more oil than we may make good in a year. What we come twenty thousand miles to get is worth saving, sir.”
“So it is, so it is; if we get it.”
“I was speaking of the oil in the hold, sir.”

“And I was not speaking or thinking of that at all. Begone! Let it leak! I’m all aleak myself. Aye! leaks in leaks! not only full of leaky casks, but those leaky casks are in a leaky ship; and that’s a far worse plight than the Pequod’s, man. Yet I don’t stop to plug my leak; for who can find it in the deep-loaded hull; or how hope to plug it, even if found, in this life’s howling gale? Starbuck! I’ll not have the Burtons hoisted.”
“What will the owners say, sir?”

“Let the owners stand on Nantucket beach and outyell the Typhoons. What cares Ahab? Owners, owners? Thou art always prating to me, Starbuck, about those miserly owners, as if the owners were my conscience. But look ye, the only real owner of anything is its commander; and hark ye, my conscience is in this ship’s keel.—On deck!”

“Captain Ahab,” said the reddening mate, moving further into the cabin, with a daring so strangely respectful and cautious that it almost seemed not only every way seeking to avoid the slightest outward manifestation of itself, but within also seemed more than half distrustful of itself; “A better man than I might well pass over in thee what he would quickly enough resent in a younger man; aye, and in a happier, Captain Ahab.”
“Devils! Dost thou then so much as dare to critically think of me?—On deck!”
“Nay, sir, not yet; I do entreat. And I do dare, sir—to be forbearing! Shall we not understand each other better than hitherto, Captain Ahab?”

Ahab seized a loaded musket from the rack (forming part of most South-Sea-men’s cabin furniture), and pointing it towards Starbuck, exclaimed: “There is one God that is Lord over the earth, and one Captain that is lord over the Pequod.—On deck!”

For an instant in the flashing eyes of the mate, and his fiery cheeks, you would have almost thought that he had really received the blaze of the levelled tube. But, mastering his emotion, he half calmly rose, and as he quitted the cabin, paused for an instant and said: “Thou hast outraged, not insulted me, sir; but for that I ask thee not to beware of Starbuck; thou wouldst but laugh; but let Ahab beware of Ahab; beware of thyself, old man.”

“He waxes brave, but nevertheless obeys; most careful bravery that!” murmured Ahab, as Starbuck disappeared. “What’s that he said—Ahab beware of Ahab—there’s something there!” Then unconsciously using the musket for a staff, with an iron brow he paced to and fro in the little cabin; but presently the thick plaits of his forehead relaxed, and returning the gun to the rack, he went to the deck.

“Thou art but too good a fellow, Starbuck,” he said lowly to the mate; then raising his voice to the crew: “Furl the t’gallant-sails, and close-reef the top-sails, fore and aft; back the main-yard; up Burton, and break out in the main-hold.”

It were perhaps vain to surmise exactly why it was, that as respecting Starbuck, Ahab thus acted. It may have been a flash of honesty in him; or mere prudential policy which, under the circumstance, imperiously forbade the slightest symptom of open disaffection, however transient, in the important chief officer of his ship. However it was, his orders were executed; and the Burtons were hoisted.

modern_en.title: Chapter 109 — Ahab and Starbuck in the Cabin
paragraphs: As usual, they were pumping out the ship the next morning, and, surprisingly, a fair amount of oil came up with the water; the casks down below must have sprung a bad leak. Everyone was very worried, and Starbuck went down to the cabin to report this bad news.*

*In sperm-whalers with any considerable quantity of oil on board, it is a regular twice-weekly duty to run a hose into the hold and drench the casks with sea-water, which is afterward removed at varying intervals by the ship's pumps. In this way the aim is to keep the casks damp and tight; while from the changed character of the water pumped out, the sailors readily detect any serious leakage in the precious cargo.

By now the Pequod was approaching Formosa and the Bashee Isles from the south and west; between them runs one of the tropical passages out of the China seas into the Pacific. So Starbuck found Ahab with a general chart of the eastern archipelagoes spread out in front of him, along with a separate one showing the long eastern coasts of the Japanese islands of Nippon, Matsumae and Shikoku. The wondrous old man, with his back to the gangway door, his snow-white new ivory leg braced against the screwed-down leg of his table and a long jackknife like a pruning-hook in his hand, was frowning and tracing out his old courses again.
"Who's there?" hearing the footstep at the door, but not turning round to it. "On deck! Begone!"
"Captain Ahab is mistaken; it is I. The oil in the hold is leaking, sir. We must hoist the Burtons (the hoisting tackles) and break out the hold."
"Hoist the Burtons and break out? Now that we are nearing Japan — heave to here for a week to tinker a parcel of old hoops?"
"It's either that, sir, or lose more oil in one day than we can make up in a year. Something we sail twenty thousand miles to get is worth saving, sir."
"So it is, so it is; if we get it."
"I was speaking of the oil in the hold, sir."

"And I wasn't speaking or thinking of that at all. Get out! Let it leak! I'm all leaks myself. Yes! Leaks within leaks! Not only full of leaky casks, but those leaky casks are in a leaky ship; and that's a far worse fix than the Pequod's, man. Yet I don't stop to plug my leak, for who can find it down in the deep-loaded hull? And even if it were found, how could anyone hope to plug it in this life's howling gale? Starbuck! I won't have the Burtons hoisted."
"What will the owners say, sir?"

"Let the owners stand on Nantucket beach and outyell the typhoons. What does Ahab care? Owners, owners? You are always prattling to me, Starbuck, about those miserly owners, as if the owners were my conscience. But look here, the only real owner of anything is its commander; and listen, my conscience is in this ship's keel. On deck!"

"Captain Ahab," said the mate, flushing as he stepped farther into the cabin. His boldness was so oddly respectful and careful that it almost seemed not only to be trying in every way to avoid the slightest outward show of itself, but also, inwardly, to be more than half unsure of itself. "A better man than I am might well overlook in you what he would be quick enough to resent in a younger man — yes, and in a happier one, Captain Ahab."
"Devils! Do you then so much as dare to think critically of me? On deck!"
"No, sir, not yet; I do beg you. And I do dare, sir — to be patient! Shall we not understand each other better than we have till now, Captain Ahab?"

Ahab seized a loaded musket from the rack — forming part of most South Sea vessels' cabin furniture — and pointing it toward Starbuck, exclaimed: "There is one God that is Lord over the earth, and one Captain that is lord over the Pequod. On deck!"

For an instant in the flashing eyes of the mate, and his fiery cheeks, you would have almost thought that he had really received the blast of the leveled barrel. But, mastering his emotion, he half-calmly rose, and as he left the cabin, paused for an instant and said: "You have outraged, not insulted me, sir; but for that I ask you not to beware of Starbuck — you would only laugh; but let Ahab beware of Ahab. Beware of yourself, old man."

"He grows brave but nevertheless obeys; that's a most careful bravery!" murmured Ahab, as Starbuck disappeared. "What's that he said — Ahab beware of Ahab — there's something there!" Then, unconsciously using the musket for a walking stick, with an iron brow he paced to and fro in the little cabin; but presently the thick furrows of his forehead relaxed, and returning the gun to the rack, he went to the deck.

"You are only too good a fellow, Starbuck," he said quietly to the mate; then, raising his voice to the crew: "Furl the topgallant-sails, and close-reef the topsails, fore and aft; back the main-yard; hoist the Burton, and break out in the main-hold."

It would perhaps be useless to guess exactly why Ahab acted this way toward Starbuck. It may have been a flash of honesty in him; or mere prudent policy which, under the circumstances, sternly forbade the slightest sign of open disaffection, however fleeting, in the important chief officer of his ship. However it was, his orders were carried out; and the Burtons were hoisted.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 109 — Ahab og Starbuck i kahytten
paragraphs: Som sædvanligt pumpede de skibet læns næste morgen, og overraskende kom en hel del olie op med vandet; tønderne dernede måtte have fået en slem lækage. Alle var meget urolige, og Starbuck gik ned i kahytten for at melde disse dårlige nyheder.*

*På kaskelotfangere med en betydelig mængde olie om bord er det en fast pligt to gange om ugen at føre en slange ned i lasten og overøse tønderne med havvand, som derefter, med forskellige mellemrum, fjernes af skibets pumper. På den måde søger man at holde tønderne fugtige og tætte; og ud fra den ændrede beskaffenhed af det vand, der pumpes op, opdager sømændene let en alvorlig lækage i den dyrebare last.

Pequod nærmede sig nu Formosa og Bashee-øerne fra syd og vest; mellem dem løber en af de tropiske passager ud af de kinesiske have og ind i Stillehavet. Så Starbuck fandt Ahab med et almindeligt kort over de østlige øhav udbredt foran sig, sammen med et særskilt kort over de japanske øers lange østkyster: Nippon, Matsumae og Shikoku. Den vidunderlige gamle mand sad med ryggen til lugedøren, sit snehvide nye elfenbensben støttet mod det fastskruede ben på sit bord og en lang foldekniv som en beskæringskniv i hånden, og med rynket pande trak han sine gamle kurser op igen.
»Hvem er det?« sagde han, da han hørte skridtet ved døren, men uden at vende sig om. »På dækket! Forsvind!«
»Kaptajn Ahab tager fejl; det er mig. Olien i lasten lækker, hr. Vi må hejse Burton-taljerne (hejsetaljerne) og bryde lasten op.«
»Hejse Burton-taljerne og bryde op? Nu, hvor vi nærmer os Japan — ligge stille her en uge for at lappe en flok gamle tøndebånd?«
»Det er enten det, hr., eller miste mere olie på en dag, end vi kan indhente på et år. Noget, vi sejler tyve tusind engelske mil for at få, er værd at redde, hr.«
»Det er det, det er det; hvis vi får det.«
»Jeg talte om olien i lasten, hr.«

»Og jeg talte eller tænkte slet ikke på den. Ud! Lad den lække! Jeg er selv fuld af lækager. Ja! Lækager inden i lækager! Ikke bare fuld af utætte tønder, men de utætte tønder ligger i et utæt skib; og det er en langt værre knibe end Pequods, mand. Alligevel stopper jeg ikke for at tætne min lækage, for hvem kan finde den dernede i det dybtlastede skrog? Og selv om den blev fundet, hvordan kunne nogen håbe at tætne den i dette livs hylende storm? Starbuck! Jeg vil ikke have Burton-taljerne hejst.«
»Hvad vil rederne sige, hr.?«

»Lad rederne stå på Nantucket-stranden og overdøve tyfonerne. Hvad bryder Ahab sig om det? Redere, redere? Du står altid og pludrer for mig om de gerrige redere, Starbuck, som om rederne var min samvittighed. Men hør her, den eneste rigtige ejer af noget er dets fører; og lyt, min samvittighed ligger i dette skibs køl. På dækket!«

»Kaptajn Ahab,« sagde styrmanden og rødmede, mens han trådte længere ind i kahytten. Hans dristighed var så underligt respektfuld og forsigtig, at den næsten så ud til ikke blot på alle måder at forsøge at undgå den mindste udvendige visning af sig selv, men også indvendig at være mere end halvt usikker på sig selv. »En bedre mand end jeg kunne sagtens overse hos Dem, hvad han hurtigt nok ville tage ilde op hos en yngre mand — ja, og en gladere, kaptajn Ahab.«
»Djævle! Vover du da overhovedet at tænke kritisk om mig? På dækket!«
»Nej, hr., ikke endnu; jeg beder Dem. Og jeg vover, hr. — at være tålmodig! Skal vi ikke forstå hinanden bedre, end vi har gjort indtil nu, kaptajn Ahab?«

Ahab greb en ladt muskedonner fra stativet — som er en del af kahytsinventaret på de fleste sydhavsskibe — og pegede den mod Starbuck og råbte: »Der er én Gud, som er herre over jorden, og én kaptajn, som er herre over Pequod. På dækket!«

Et øjeblik kunne man næsten i styrmandens flammende øjne og glødende kinder have troet, at han virkelig havde fået skuddet fra det rettede løb. Men han beherskede sig, rejste sig halvt roligt, og da han forlod kahytten, standsede han et øjeblik og sagde: »De har krænket mig, ikke fornærmet mig, hr.; men for det beder jeg Dem ikke om at passe på Starbuck — De ville bare le; men lad Ahab passe på Ahab. Pas på Dem selv, gamle mand.«

»Han bliver modig, men adlyder alligevel; det er en meget forsigtig tapperhed!« mumlede Ahab, da Starbuck forsvandt. »Hvad var det, han sagde — Ahab pas på Ahab — der er noget i det!« Så brugte han uvilkårligt musketten som stok og gik med jernpande frem og tilbage i den lille kahyt; men snart løsnede panden sine tykke furer, og han stillede geværet tilbage i stativet og gik op på dækket.

»Du er bare alt for god en fyr, Starbuck,« sagde han stille til styrmanden; så hævede han stemmen til mandskabet: »Beslå bramsejlene og tag dybe rev i mærssejlene, for og agter; bak stor-råen; hejs Burton-taljen og bryd op i storlasten.«

Det er måske nytteløst at gætte på, hvorfor Ahab handlede sådan over for Starbuck. Det kan have været et glimt af ærlighed hos ham. Eller det kan have været ren og skær klog politik, som under de givne omstændigheder strengt forbød selv det mindste tegn på åbenlys utilfredshed, hvor flygtigt det end var, hos skibets vigtige første styrmand. Hvordan det end var, blev hans ordrer udført, og Burton-taljerne blev hejst.
